messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] covariates in distance sampling
parts:
hi Phil,

 (1) The 2nd approach is an ad hoc attempt to do the 1st approach (i.e., joint estimation of all the parameters together in the same likelihood).  doing the 2nd approach will generally be less efficient statistically and produce biased estimates of standard errors and possibly parameters in some cases.

 (2) no.

 (3) no rules of thumb here. the usual considerations apply (bias/variance trade-off, over-fitting, identifiability, instability of the likelihood, etc..)

regards
andy




From: Phil Shirk <fil...@gmail.com>
To: unma...@googlegroups.com
Date: 08/30/2012 09:21 AM
Subject: [unmarked] covariates in distance sampling
Sent by: unma...@googlegroups.com




Hello, I have a number of general and specific questions regarding covariates in distance-based density estimation, and welcome answers, suggestions, or a nudge in the right direction.  

1) What are differences (advantages, disadvantages) of including covariates as part of the original density estimates rather than doing a simple density estimates, using the effective area sampled to calculate a density estimate for each transect, and then using multiple regression to determine the impacts of covariates on densities?

2) Are covariates assumed to be normally distributed?  If so, how important is this assumption?  

3) How many covariates is 'too many'/helpful?  Just run lots and compare AIC's?

Thanks in advance,
Phil
